subject: Banking
title: Digital Currencies from Central Banks
description: A micro-lesson that makes Digital Currencies from Central Banks usable.

hook.text: Over 130 countries are developing central bank digital currencies.

buildup.text: CBDCs would let citizens hold accounts directly at the central bank. No commercial bank needed as an intermediary.

discovery.text: Instant, free payments between anyone with a CBDC wallet. No Visa, no Swift, no clearing delays.

twist.text: CBDCs give governments total visibility into spending. Every transaction recorded.

climax.text: CBDCs offer efficiency at the cost of privacy. The future of money depends on how that tradeoff is resolved.

punchline.text: 130 countries exploring digital money. Efficiency vs. privacy is the battle.

quiz.question: What is a major concern about CBDCs?
options: Governments could track every transaction, eliminating financial privacy

details.summary: Central bank digital currencies are government-issued digital money that could replace physical cash, offering instant settlement and programmable features while giving central banks unprecedented visibility into transactions.
details.whyItMatters: CBDCs could transform how money works, enabling instant payments and financial inclusion. But they also raise profound privacy concerns by giving governments the ability to monitor and control every transaction.
takeaways: China's digital yuan is the most advanced major CBDC project
CBDCs could eliminate the need for commercial bank deposits for payments
Privacy concerns are the primary obstacle in democratic countries

faq.question: How is a CBDC different from money in a bank app?
faq.answer: Bank app balances are IOUs from a commercial bank. A CBDC is a direct claim on the central bank, making it as safe as physical cash. It eliminates counterparty risk and could enable instant settlement without intermediaries.

faq.question: Could governments use CBDCs to surveil citizens?
faq.answer: Yes, that is the primary concern. Unlike cash, every CBDC transaction could be tracked. Democracies are exploring privacy-preserving designs, but authoritarian regimes could use CBDCs for financial surveillance and control.
